section_1.title: Defining the Vector: Magnitude and Direction
section_1.content: Introduce a vector as a directed arrow representing both magnitude (length) and direction. Contrast this with scalars (simple numbers).
section_1.example: A squirrel running 5 meters North-East; the arrow represents the displacement.

section_2.title: Visualization via Coordinate Systems
section_2.content: Explain how to place vectors on a 2D Cartesian plane (x, y). Define components as the horizontal and vertical 'steps' taken to reach the tip of the arrow from the tail.
section_2.example: Representing a robot's movement as (3, 4), meaning 3 units right and 4 units up on a grid.

section_3.title: Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Rule
section_3.content: Demonstrate the geometric method of adding vectors by placing the tail of the second vector at the tip of the first. Explain that the result (resultant) is the direct path from start to finish.
section_3.example: A boat traveling East, then diverted by a river current South; the resultant arrow shows the actual path relative to the shore.

section_4.title: Scalar Multiplication: Scaling Reality
section_4.content: Show how multiplying a vector by a scalar constant changes its length without changing its original orientation (unless the scalar is negative).
section_4.example: A superhero jumping: if vector 'v' is a jump, '2v' is a jump twice as long in the exact same direction.

section_5.title: Summary and Real-World Application
section_5.content: Briefly synthesize how vectors simplify complex movements in gaming engines and physics simulations by breaking them down into manageable coordinate components.
section_5.example: A video game character jumping: velocity vectors are calculated using these exact component additions to determine landing coordinates.
